title: Test doubles and mocking
idea: A test double is a stand-in object you pass where a real dependency would go, so a unit test runs fast, repeatably and without the outside world.

analogy.text: A film shoot uses a stunt double for the dangerous scene and a cardboard prop in the background. Each stands in for one job only.
analogy.breaks: A film double is unseen; a test may inspect what the double saw.

points: Dummy fills a parameter; stub returns canned answers; fake is a working in-memory version.
A spy records calls for later checks; a mock knows expected calls upfront.
Doubles are easiest when a class receives its dependencies, ideally interfaces, through its constructor.
Prefer checking state through fakes; mock only where the call itself is the behaviour.

messages.label: new Checkout(stub, fake, spy, dummy)
messages.note: Arrange: the test builds the class with doubles. The dummy audit log is passed but must never be called.

messages.label: pay("O-1", 1999)
messages.note: Act: one call to the class under test.

messages.label: charge("O-1", 1999)
messages.note: The stub ignores its inputs. No network, no card, no flakiness.

messages.label: true
messages.note: It returns the canned answer the test chose: approved.

messages.label: save("O-1", PAID)
messages.note: The fake really stores the row, in a map instead of a database.

messages.label: send("O-1")
messages.note: The spy sends nothing. It only writes the call down.

messages.label: status("O-1")?
messages.note: Assert on state: ask the fake what was saved.

messages.label: sent()?
messages.note: Assert on the interaction that matters: exactly one receipt, for O-1.

code.title: Stub, fake, spy and dummy
code.caption: Hand-written doubles test both payment outcomes in milliseconds, with no gateway, database or mail server.

walk.text: Each dependency is an interface, so any stand-in can be plugged in.
Constructor injection: the class never creates its collaborators itself.
Stubs as lambdas: one canned answer each, chosen by the test.
The fake is a real store backed by a map; tests read its state.
The spy records each call; `sent` exposes a copy for assertions.
The dummy fails loudly if touched, proving the happy path skips auditing.
Assertions check outcomes: saved status and who got a receipt.

code.title: When a mock over-specifies
code.caption: A refactor batches receipts. Customers see no change, yet the strict mock fails while the fake-based test passes.

walk.text: Two versions with identical results: one call per order, or one batch call.
The mock holds an exact script of expected calls and compares afterwards.
The mock test passes for v1 and breaks on v2: it tested how, not what.
The fake keeps the outcome: which orders received a receipt.
The state test passes for both versions, so the refactor stays safe.

pitfalls: Mocking every collaborator makes tests fail on harmless refactors while real bugs still pass.
Mocking types you do not own, like a vendor SDK, tests your guess of its behaviour.
A stub returning the value the test asserts proves only that the stub works.

quiz.q: A class sends an SMS alert after a failed login. Which double should test it?
options: A dummy, since SMS is outside the unit
A spy that records the alert sent
A stub returning the SMS gateway's status code
The real SMS client pointed at a test number
quiz.why: Sending the alert is the behaviour itself, so the test must see the call. A spy records it; a dummy or stub cannot, and real SMS is slow and costly.

takeaway: Stub inputs, fake stores, spy on effects; mock sparingly.
